claim: Editions are spelled out and lowercased ('fifth edition'), with 4E/5E abbreviations confined to tables, conversion documents, or informal text.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: We write “fifth edition,” for instance, not “5th Edition.”

verdict.trueWording: we spell out and lowercase references to editions
verdict.note: Same PDF, rule spans p.1-p.2: "Editions of the RPG. In a departure from previous usage, we spell out and lowercase references to editions of the roleplaying game. We write “fifth edition,” for instance, not “5th Edition.” ... Our internal documentation occasionally uses edition abbreviations like 4E and 5E. In other contexts, such abbreviations should appear only in a table, a conversion document, or in an informal text." Quote verbatim on p.2 as cited; both limbs supported. The page adds one carve-out the claim omits: internal documentation itself does use 4E/5E.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the claim's 'confined to tables, conversion documents, or informal text' omits the guide's own carve-out that internal documentation does use 4E/5E

claim: v1.08a newly permits singular 'they/their' but tells writers to reach for it only when no other pleasing alternative exists.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: but don’t abuse this liberty

verdict.trueWording: Rely on it only lacking a reasonable or pleasing alternative
verdict.note: p.2: 'In a departure from our past usage, we allow the use of "they" and "their" as singular pronouns, but don't abuse this liberty. Rely on this device only when you have no other reasonable or pleasing alternative.' Quote verbatim. The 'newly' limb rests on the page's own 'In a departure from our past usage' in a document stamped 'Version 1.08a'; the page never says the change was introduced at 1.08a specifically.

claim: In 2019 'man' and 'woman' were reserved for humans only, so a dwarf is a 'male dwarf', never a 'dwarf man'.

verdict.note: p.2 'Gender and Fantasy Races': '"Man," "woman," and their plurals are reserved for describing humans only. For example, we write "male dwarf," not "dwarf man" or "man dwarf."' Rule and quote verbatim. The '2019' dating is not on the page — every footer reads 'Version 1.08a (c)2018 Wizards of the Coast'; the January 2019 update date comes from the hosting file name, as the claim's own source field records.

verdict.trueWording: Priestess only if part of a person's or in-world title
verdict.note: p.3 'Gender-Specific Suffixes': 'Avoid gender-specific suffixes whenever possible. For example, we write "priest" or "actor" whether the person is male or female. Use a word like "priestess" or "actress" only if it's part of a person's title or an in-world organizations' titles.' claim: Bold is the only emphasis device, and a term already in the section heading gets no emphasis in running text.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: Use bold for such emphasis

verdict.unsupportedLimb: that bold is the ONLY emphasis device - the page prescribes bold for emphasis in place of an inline subhead, and nowhere states or implies that it is the sole permitted emphasis device
verdict.trueWording: Use bold for such emphasis, unless it's in the heading
verdict.note: p.3: 'Finally, don't use an inline subhead when you simply want to emphasize a word or phrase. Use bold for such emphasis, unless the emphasized term or phrase appears in the section's heading. Then, no emphasis is required. For example, if a Heading 3 says "Ki Points," don't bold "ki points" in the associated running text.' Quote verbatim and the heading-term limb fully supported; the exclusivity quantifier 'only' is the claim's, not the guide's - the guide's italics rules elsewhere (pp.4, 6-7) govern titles, spells, words-as-words and unspoken discourse, and it never rules italics out for emphasis in so many words.

claim: Sidebars are rationed; any sidebar that must follow a specific passage to make sense should be folded into body text instead.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: The best sidebars can appear anywhere on a page

verdict.trueWording: If it must follow a section to be intelligible, probably not a sidebar
verdict.note: p.3 'Sidebars': 'Avoid overusing sidebars. If a sidebar must follow a particular section of text to be intelligible, it probably shouldn't be a sidebar. The best sidebars can appear anywhere on a page and still make sense.' Quote verbatim; both limbs supported, with the guide hedging 'probably shouldn't be a sidebar' and leaving the remedy (body text) implicit rather than naming it.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the body-text remedy is the claimant's: the guide hedges 'it probably shouldn't be a sidebar' and leaves the remedy unnamed

claim: In D&D fiction, thoughts and psionic speech may be set in italics, quotes, or plain type at the author's discretion, a reversal of the older policy.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: Aesthetics and clarity should dictate appropriate usage

verdict.trueWording: a change from our previous policy
verdict.note: Quote 'Aesthetics and clarity should dictate appropriate usage' is verbatim on p.6, and the discretion limbs are fully supported: 'In D&D fiction, authors are free to use italics, quotation marks, or no distinguishing typography to present a character's thoughts or psionic communication (see Chicago 13.43).' But the page says only '(This is a change from our previous policy.)' — the word 'reversal' is absent, and the guide never states what the previous policy was, so the claim's characterization of the direction of the change is not established by the page.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: 'a reversal of the older policy' — page says only 'a change from our previous policy' and never states the prior rule

claim: 'Magic' is the adjective for objects (magic item, magic sword); 'magical' for other things; 'magical item' is forbidden.
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.08a (2018; 'updated January 2019')
quote: “magic item” and its variants should never be “magical item.”

verdict.trueWording: Magic for objects; magical used more often for other things; never magical item
verdict.note: Quote exact on p.8. Limbs 1 and 3 are verbatim rules ('a magic item, a magic sword, a magic trap'; 'should never be "magical item"'). Limb 2 is a preference, not an absolute, in the source: 'The adjective can be used for other things, but we use "magical" more often than "magic" for them' — the claim's clean split states the guide's default correctly but drops the 'more often' hedge.
verdict.unsupportedLimb: the 'magical for other things' half is a preference, not the absolute the claim's clean split states: 'we use "magical" more often than "magic" for them'

claim: Sections absent from v1.04a and present in v1.08a include Gender-Specific Suffixes, Headings, Sidebars, Bulleted Lists, Appendix References, and Adventuring Parties (verified by heading presence in both texts).
source: D&D Style Guide: Writing and Editing, Version 1.04a (2013)

verdict.trueWording: Five of the six are new headings; 'Bulleted Lists' renames v1.04a's 'Vertical Lists'.
verdict.note: Both raw texts extracted and grepped. Heading-string counts: Gender-Specific Suffixes 0/2, Headings 0/4, Sidebars 0/3, Bulleted Lists 0/1, Appendix References 0/1, Adventuring Parties 0/1 (2013/2019). v1.04a's full heading roster was enumerated and contains none of the six strings; its only 'sidebar'/'heading' mentions are passing references inside 'Subsection/Table References' and 'Inline Subheads', and it has zero occurrences of 'appendix', 'appendices', 'suffix' or 'fellowship'. So five limbs are genuinely new sections; the sixth is a rename, which the claim's word 'Sections' over-states even though its parenthetical scopes verification to heading presence. No quote field, so VERBATIM is inapplicable in any case.

claim: Men and women are depicted equally in all roles; sexist clichés (damsel, sexy barmaid) are banned, with orcs and Northlanders as the two exceptions.
source: Forgotten Realms Style Guide (Wizards of the Coast, bundle document)
quote: Avoid clichés that reinforce sexist

verdict.trueWording: Males and females depicted in equal measure; two exceptions.
verdict.note: p.2 'Gender Roles': quote exact. 'males and females should be depicted in equal measure and doing all the same jobs in equal status'; cliche list names 'the damsel in distress, the sexy barmaid'; 'There are two exceptions: orcs and Northlanders.' Guide word is 'Avoid', not 'banned'; the two exceptions as elaborated concern gendered division of labour (orc females stay behind, Northlander women stay home), not licence to use the cliches.

verdict.note: p.1, guideline 3: 'Stay experiential. Don’t attempt to use exposition to explain everything in the IP, but do inform the players about the world.' The two-word quote is exact and the experiential limb holds, but the claim drops both the 'everything' quantifier and the mandatory counter-clause, converting a calibrated instruction into a blanket prohibition the page contradicts.
